title: Did Caesar Really Say "Et tu, Brute?" What the Ancient Sources Actually Wrote
description:
In Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, Caesar first says the Latin "Et tu, Brute?", then the English "Then fall, Caesar!", and only then comes the stage direction for his death. The same passage of Suetonius first says that he uttered no words as he was stabbed, only a groan at the first blow, and then keeps a Greek version that "some writers have handed down"; Plutarch's two biographies do not vouch for the Latin line. This episode separates the ancient biographies' own text, a later translator's footnote and lines written for the stage, and asks how far this famous quotation can really be confirmed. The visuals are AI cartoon illustrations, not footage of the historical events. Information checked on 2026-10-20.

Sources:
Suetonius, Divus Iulius 80–85 (PerseusDL Rolfe Latin): https://github.com/PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit/blob/128a05afa9cc7179ab18f8d05f78a9f1dd50e415/data/phi1348/abo011/phi1348.abo011.rolfe-lat1.xml#L587-L638
Plutarch, Caesar and Brutus: https://github.com/GITenberg/Plutarch-Lives-of-the-noble-Grecians-and-Romans_674/blob/6aea7c6d83ee3596f9106d2d832d705aa4ed4620/674.txt#L46821-L46946
Brutus section: https://github.com/GITenberg/Plutarch-Lives-of-the-noble-Grecians-and-Romans_674/blob/6aea7c6d83ee3596f9106d2d832d705aa4ed4620/674.txt#L63906-L64180

thumbnail.headline: **Who wrote it?**
thumbnail.sub: The ancient text says something else

chapters.cs001: An actor opens his mouth; Caesar has not yet fallen
chapters.cs007: Two Brutuses walk into the Curia of Pompey
chapters.cs017: Decimus talks Caesar out of the house
chapters.cs034: Cimber grabs the toga, Casca draws
chapters.cs049: Suetonius leaves another line at the end of the passage
chapters.cs064: Shakespeare gives the actor a Latin question
chapters.cs076: An editor puts a Latin guess in a footnote

cs001.text: On a wooden stage, the actor playing Caesar sits down; another suddenly closes in.

cs002.text: The actor playing Brutus raises a prop dagger. Freeze, before Caesar speaks.

cs003.text: This script gives him a line. Do the ancient biographies record the same words?

cs004.text: Before that meeting, someone handed him a warning. Did he read it?

cs005.text: That day had two Brutuses. One talked him into going out. Where would the other stand?

cs006.text: Let's freeze the stage here: what did the real Caesar last say?

cs007.text: On Suetonius's list of conspirators, both Marcus and Decimus bear the name Brutus.

cs008.text: This biography says more than sixty men were in the plot.

cs009.text: They weighed the elections, the streets, a theater entrance, then chose a Senate meeting.

cs010.text: On March 15, the senators were to meet in Pompey's assembly hall.

cs011.text: The hall stood beside Pompey's theater, as Plutarch also notes. Would Caesar make it to his seat?

cs012.text: Meanwhile, words mocking Caesar as a would-be king appeared under his statue.

cs013.text: Even Marcus's own judgment seat got anonymous notes urging him to act.

cs014.text: Plutarch says the other plotters wanted Marcus's name to give the deed weight.

cs015.text: Decimus had joined the plot too, yet Caesar still trusted him.

cs016.text: Which of the two would personally lead Caesar out of his house?

cs017.text: On the morning of March 15, before that Brutus came, Caesar thought of staying home.

cs018.text: Suetonius mentions he was unwell, and that the omens were bad.

cs019.text: Plutarch writes that Calpurnia even urged her husband to postpone.

cs020.text: Dreams and omens are just stories in the biographies. Could they stop Caesar?

cs021.text: Then the other Brutus pressed him: the senators were waiting, don't waste the whole session.

cs022.text: Caesar listened and left his house.

cs023.text: The Brutus who talked him into going was Decimus.

cs024.text: On the way, Caesar was handed a plot warning.

cs025.text: He tucked it among other papers in his hand, to read later.

cs026.text: Plutarch also tells of that warning, but says the crowd kept him from reading it all.

cs027.text: The warning reached him but didn't stop him. Who waited at the hall?

cs028.text: The plotters waited in Pompey's portico; Caesar's delay made them nervous.

cs029.text: A senator quietly told Marcus and Cassius he hoped they'd finish quickly.

cs030.text: They feared they'd been exposed; when he went to talk to Caesar, they grew tenser.

cs031.text: Watching the man's face, Marcus judged he was only pleading with Caesar.

cs032.text: Another plotter kept Antony talking outside.

cs033.text: Caesar went in and sat; a petitioner came right up. What would he say first?

cs034.text: It was Tillius Cimber, pleading for his exiled brother.

cs035.text: Caesar refused, so Cimber seized his toga.

cs036.text: Suetonius records Caesar's first cry: "This is violence!"

cs037.text: That came before the first blow, not the famous last question.

cs038.text: Then one of the Cascas struck. Could Caesar still fight back?

cs039.text: Caesar grabbed his arm; Suetonius says he struck back with a stylus.

cs040.text: Plutarch's Life of Caesar has him, after the first blow, rebuke Casca in Latin.

cs041.text: The two biographies give Caesar different words at different moments.

cs042.text: Casca then called to his brother for help, in Greek, Plutarch says.

cs043.text: That Greek was Casca's. Did Caesar himself speak Greek later on?

cs044.text: Nearby senators froze in shock, neither fleeing nor helping.

cs045.text: Caesar tried to get out, but drawn blades ringed him.

cs046.text: Plutarch's Life of Brutus says Marcus stood before him, dagger in hand.

cs047.text: So Caesar let go of Casca's arm and covered his head with his toga.

cs048.text: Now it was Marcus before him. Did ancient writers give Caesar a last line?

cs049.text: Suetonius first writes that through twenty-three blows, Caesar uttered no words.

cs050.text: He records only one groan, at the first blow.

cs051.text: But this Latin passage doesn't end with the groan.

cs052.text: He goes on: though some have handed down another saying.

cs053.text: He names no one, and never claims he was there to hear it.

cs054.text: In that story, as Marcus Brutus rushed at him, Caesar spoke to him.

cs055.text: Three Greek words, roughly: "You too, child?"

cs056.text: The words themselves don't name Brutus; the name is in the author's lead-in.

cs057.text: Nor does "child" prove a blood tie between them.

cs058.text: Would Plutarch, the other biographer, back up those three Greek words?

cs059.text: Plutarch's Caesar cites one account: he fell at the foot of Pompey's statue.

cs060.text: That passage gives him no last words for Marcus.

cs061.text: In the Life of Brutus, after Caesar falls, Marcus tries to explain; no one listens.

cs062.text: Both are by the same author: not two independent eyewitnesses.

cs063.text: Silence isn't proof it never happened. So who wrote the Latin line into a script?

cs064.text: Back to the frozen stage: now the actor playing Caesar speaks on.

cs065.text: Shakespeare's petitioners crowd in; Caesar says he's constant as the northern star.

cs066.text: Casca cries, "Speak, hands, for me!" and a stage direction has him and the rest stab.

cs067.text: The script makes a point of having Marcus Brutus stab him too.

cs068.text: In the famous line that follows, only "Et tu, Brute?" is in Latin.

cs069.text: His next words, "Then fall, Caesar!", are English in this text.

cs070.text: That's Caesar's last spoken line in the script; only then comes the direction "Dies."

cs071.text: The actor has clear words and actions. Do the ancient texts give that same Latin question?

cs072.text: But no ancient writer left that Latin question with such certainty.

cs073.text: The play proves Shakespeare wrote it, not that Caesar ever said it.

cs074.text: And the play doesn't prove Shakespeare was the first to write it either.

cs075.text: Later, an English Twelve Caesars even put a Latin guess in a footnote. What gets misread?

cs076.text: That translation renders the address as "my son," not Shakespeare's "Brutus."

cs077.text: That line carries note 97; turn to the footnote, and another language appears.

cs078.text: There, a later editor guesses Caesar likely spoke it in Latin.

cs079.text: The footnote has no word-for-word record; "very likely" shows it's the editor's guess.

cs080.text: The editor also finds the translated address too long for a crisis.

cs081.text: His own reasoning: in a crisis like that, why would Caesar switch to Greek?

cs082.text: It notes manuscript variants in Greek letters, but cites no ancient copy with the Latin line.

cs083.text: It's the editor's reasoning, not words for Suetonius's mouth. What does the Latin really say?

cs084.text: The biography's Latin original has no trace of the Latin line the editor guessed.

cs085.text: Back to our opening question: we can be sure of the script, but not that Caesar said that Latin line.

cs086.text: Next time, ask of a famous quote: ancient text, a translation's footnote, or the stage?

cs999a.text: History may leave no clear last words; drama can leave a line everyone knows.

cs999b.text: Where did you first hear this line: in a textbook, a movie, or a play?

cs999c.text: To keep tracing famous moments in history back to the sources, subscribe to the channel.
